title: Safety Warning: Carborane Mixtures
body_text: Here’s a paper that I thought deserved a bit more notice than it’s probably getting - there are people who could use to see it who probably don’t read Inorganic Chemistry very often. It’s about carboranes, which are interesting-looking cage-type clusters of boron and carbon atoms. These come in a number of varieties, and they’ve been looked at in several fields of chemistry - inorganic, materials science, but there are even applications in medicinal chemistry. That’s because of all those boron atoms - these are able to capture low-energy neutrons (the neutron cross section of a boron -10 atom is orders of magnitude higher than the other elements in biochemistry). And when that happens, a high-energy alpha particle is emitted, causing great destruction around a very small area. This means that if you have a boron-containing molecule that happens to concentrate in tumor tissue, you have a very interesting opportunity to do severe damage to the tumor cells while sparing those around it. This is a neat idea that has proven difficult to realize in practice, partly due to getting good neutron sources and partly due to getting good boron-containing compounds with the right distribution profiles. But boron-rich groups like carboranes are very good candidates for refining the latter part of the problem, and a lot of work has gone into that over the years. And that’s all fine, but the new paper linked in the first paragraph points out something that I don’t think people have realized: the widely used ortho-carborane can be an explosion hazard when mixed with a surprising number of other materials. The work apparently kicked off with an observation that a mixture of the carborane and good ol’ sodium sulfate was actually explosively sensitive to mechanical force. That’s quite a surprise, since neither component by itself is. So the authors surveyed mixtures with many other salts and materials and uncovered a rather alarming number of things to look out for. The traditional oxidizers caused trouble, and that was something one might have anticipated (or perhaps not, given ortho-carborane’s reputation for inertness). Nitrates of all sorts, perchlorates, manganese dioxide, all of these turn out to sensitize the carborane. But so does sodium sulfate, as observed, as well as sodium triflate and sodium azide. Now that last one you might not feel is a surprise, but azide fans know that sodium azide is not actually considered to be an impact explosion hazard by itself. But its mixture with ortho-carborane is! The mechanism for this problem is as yet unknown, but the order of sensitization does follow the reduction potentials of the additives, as you might well expect. Other carborane isomers behave quite similarly, by the way. As a practical matter, the authors note that with the ones that truly led to explosive mixtures that there was no middle ground: if they were bad, they were very bad indeed, with impact sensitivities worse than (say) lead azide or pentaerythritol tetranitrate (PETN). That should raise the eyebrows of any experienced chemists: these are very well-known primary explosives, and “worse than that by impact and friction” is not a category you want to find yourself exploring. “For safe handling of these mixtures,” say the authors, “the best recommendation is not to handle them whatsoever”. Nonfunctionalized carboranes appear to be fine. But since there’s no way of knowing yet how far this phenomenon extends, it would be wise to be very careful with any mixtures of carboranes with oxidizers or metal salts in general. Forewarned is forearmed - or in this case, forearmored.
